headline: Post-blow shelf break opens up east of the Hudson — yellowfin on the warm seam
subhead: A widened thermal edge and a darkening moon set up the best canyon window of the season, while bluefin stack the 20-fathom breaks closer to home.
body_markdown:
Last week beat us up before it paid us back. We had a blow roll through that put a chop on Veatch and Hydrographer that nobody with sense wanted to run into, and for three days the fleet sat at the dock watching the forecast instead of the water. But blows do something out here that flat calm never does — they mix the shelf water and sharpen the edges. When it finally laid down Tuesday night, the boats that got out found a shelf-slope thermal break pushing 10.3 degrees Fahrenheit, the widest differential we've seen all season. That's not a subtle seam. That's a wall you can practically see on the plotter before you see it in the water color.

This week the moon is sliding toward new, which means darker nights and building current — good for the squid-light program on bluefin, tougher on slack-tide structure bites closer to the beach. Tides are building toward the new-moon springs that peak around the 11th through 13th, and that's going to matter more for the guys working the 20-fathom breaks than it will out at the canyons, where the tuna don't care much what the tide is doing at Montauk Point. Water temps on the shelf have been climbing with the second warming surge off Georges Bank, and that's re-energized the Veatch/Hydrographer differential after a stretch where the two canyons were running nearly identical and giving us no reason to pick one over the other. Now there's a reason again.

Wednesday and Thursday were the first real post-blow window and the fleet made the most of it. Yellowfin on the 100-fathom line, working the warm seam between Wilmington and Poor Man's and pushing up the Hudson east wall. Sizes have been mixed — some quality 60-to-80-pound fish mixed with smaller schoolies that show up in pockets and then vanish. The pattern that's worked is trolling a spread of ballyhoo with green machines and small Joe Baggs-style minnows on the shortest lines to mimic the sand eel and squid bait that's been thick on the meter, then switching to spinning gear with stickbaits and poppers the moment you see birds working or fish showing on top. Don't troll through a surface push — stop short, cast into it, and let the fish come to you. That's cost me fish in years past when I plowed straight into a school with four rods in the water instead of pulling back and picking up a popper rod.

Bigeye have been mixed in with the yellowfin on the same warm seam, mostly on the night bite — drift a rigged squid or a big Illex-style jig down under the boat once the sun's down and the current's moving, and don't be shocked if it's a bigeye instead of the yellowfin you were expecting. The squid have been the story all season out here — thick on the sounder, and that's exactly why the tuna have been willing to sit on structure instead of just roaming open water like they did earlier in the season.

Closer to the beach, the bluefin story is the one I'd chase if I only had a day boat and not the fuel budget for a full canyon run. The northeast upwelling this week has sharpened the 20-to-30 fathom breaks, and the corridor out toward Coimbra has bluefin sitting right on the structure at around 20 fathoms. With the moon going dark, the overnight squid-light program is going to be the right call — get out there before dusk, get your lights down, and let the squid stack up under the hull. Once they're thick, switch to jigging or a lightly weighted live squid under a balloon. It's not a fast bite, but it's a real one, and it beats burning four hours each way to the canyon for a coin-flip day.

White marlin haven't shown yet on our side of the ledger. The warm plume that's supposed to trigger the first flags is still pushing toward the bank, and historically that shows up on the mid-Atlantic canyons before it ever reaches us. I wouldn't rig for marlin out of Montauk or Block Island yet — I'd keep the spread tuna-focused and treat any marlin shot as a bonus, not a plan.

Wahoo and mahi have been incidental so far — a few mahi picked up around lobster gear and weedlines on the way out, nothing organized enough to call a pattern. If you're running out anyway, keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small stickbait for anything holding under floating debris. Costs you nothing and it's paid off more than once for me on the ride out.

Looking ahead, the fuel math still rules this beat. From Montauk, Veatch is the shorter run and it's carrying the better thermal setup right now with that Georges Bank surge feeding it — that's where I'd point the bow if I only had one shot this week. If the seas build again with the new moon current, I'd rather work the closer bluefin corridor at night than fight a long slog to Hydrographer in building swell. Best case, that shelf edge holds through the weekend and the yellowfin stay stacked on the warm seam — I've seen that happen before when a strong post-blow break sets up this clean. If it slides or the water mixes back down, I'd shift effort to the bluefin breaks and wait for the next window. Either way, check the swell forecast before you commit fuel — the canyon bite is real right now, but it's only worth the run if the ocean lets you fish it comfortably once you get there.
